For this reason, in this second part, Chapter I will discuss its purpose and its subject.
Second, misunderstandings can arise concerning the method of Phenomenology.
Phenomenology is defined as a dialectical introduction to philosophy. If we are not careful, we may therefore assume that its method is itself dialectical.
In fact, it is its object—and only its object—that is dialectical.
For this reason, Chapter II of this second part will discuss dialectic in general and the phenomenological method.
Third, the structure of a Phenomenology is especially important.
In other branches of knowledge, the order of presentation may make something easier or harder to understand, but it does not usually distort the content itself.
In Phenomenology, by contrast, misunderstanding the order of presentation can lead directly to misunderstanding the Phenomenology itself.
The main reason is that two different orders intersect within it: a logical order and a chronological order. These must therefore be kept rigorously distinct.
For this reason, I will also discuss the structure of Phenomenology in this part, in Chapter III.
But I repeat: everything said in this first, introductory volume can be accepted as true or rejected as false only after the book has been understood and judged as a whole.
Everything said here has just one purpose: to make the book easier to understand and, by doing so, easier to judge.
I. The purpose, theme, and object of a Phenomenology

I have already stressed several times that the “revised and corrected edition” of the great Hegel’s Phenomenology that I am proposing—like the work of the same name written by Marx’s master—is not an end in itself. The aim of Hegel’s Phenomenology is “wisdom,” or, as he calls it, “science”: the complete system of true knowledge. The aim of my Phenomenology, by contrast, is philosophy in the narrower sense: a system of true but partial, and therefore imperfect, knowledge, which is to provide the material from which the structure of perfect knowledge can eventually be built. Hegel therefore sees his Phenomenology as the path that leads step by step to wisdom. My Phenomenology claims only to be the path that leads step by step to philosophy—and to wisdom only insofar as this philosophy itself leads there. In other words, if we define a Phenomenology by its aim, we can call it an introduction to philosophy.

As for the theme and subject of a Phenomenology, these are the being that actually strives toward philosophy and wisdom. Since the human being is the only being of this kind, a Phenomenology can be defined as a “discourse on the human being,” that is, an anthropology. And since the author of the Phenomenology is himself striving, above all, toward the philosophy to which that Phenomenology is supposed to lead, it can in a certain sense also be regarded as his philosophical autobiography. Its theme and subject are therefore not the human being “in general,” but the concrete human being who is actually writing it.
Let us begin with a few words about the aim of Phenomenology, that is, about its relation to philosophy.

The aim of Hegel’s Phenomenology is nothing other than the complete system of true knowledge: perfect knowledge, omniscience, or, in a word, “wisdom.” But from our present point of view, wisdom is not yet attainable. We can only “approach” it. In other words, only philosophy is currently possible. Philosophy can therefore become the aim of our Phenomenology.

As a rule, we call something an aim not when it already exists, but when it is something that is still to come into being as the result of actions directed toward it. We can therefore say that, when an author begins writing a Phenomenology, he assumes that true philosophy does not yet exist. At the same time, once a Phenomenology has been written, it becomes precisely the necessary condition that makes the appearance of this philosophy possible. We could equally say that the aim of a Phenomenology is to transform non-philosophy into philosophy.
Who, then, is this “pre-phenomenological” non-philosopher whom the Phenomenology is supposed to turn into a philosopher?

With their usual “presumption,” people who write about philosophy normally imagine this non-philosopher simply as a reader. “Introductions to philosophy” are supposedly written for him, because the philosopher himself has no need of them. The philosopher can already read—and in fact does read—any philosophical work without requiring a handbook to prepare him for it. But the “naive” reader, who knows nothing about philosophy and has not been trained in it, may fail to understand the philosophical works placed before him. He therefore has to be prepared. He has to learn the language of philosophy, be shown its aims and methods, and so on. And for that purpose he needs to read some kind of Introduction to Philosophy.

The need for such an “introduction” is indeed undeniable. Philosophy has to be learned, just like any other field of knowledge. Contrary to a fairly common belief, a serious philosophical treatise is no more accessible to a beginner than a book of advanced mathematics is to someone with no mathematical training.

The difficulty is not merely a matter of terminology. Technical terms such as “substance,” “subject,” “object,” and so on are certainly useful, but one could in principle do without them. The real difficulty is a lack of practice: the reader is not yet accustomed to thinking philosophically—to asking questions, discussing them, and answering them in a certain way.

From my point of view, the Phenomenology we are considering here is precisely this kind of necessary “introduction to philosophy.” It is meant to be the entrance—or, more exactly, the path—by which an ordinary person can make his way into philosophy itself.

This certainly does not mean that it can be read like a novel. It is not a book for small children, nor a school textbook, and it is certainly not intended for someone looking for “easy and entertaining knowledge.” On the contrary, reading it requires sustained and intense concentration, as well as a fairly high level of general education. But a reader who has reached that level should be able to read it without any previous philosophical training.

The book can therefore—and hopes to—be the reader’s first philosophical book. Once he has finished it, he should in principle be adequately prepared to read any philosophical work. Above all, he will have acquired what he needs in order to read the systematic philosophy that is supposed to follow from this Phenomenology and to be built upon it.
In short, a Phenomenology is supposed to make this Philosophy accessible to everyone.
But we must strongly emphasize that this “accessibility” matters not only to the non-philosophical reader. It matters even more to the author of the philosophy himself.

On the one hand, as we already know, philosophy seeks to bring about a conscious life. It is therefore natural that the philosopher should address himself not only to “intellectuals” in general and to his “colleagues” in particular—people who tend to think and talk about life more than they actually live and act—but also, and above all, to people engaged in real everyday activity, who usually have no special philosophical training.

On the other hand, as we have already seen and will see again, a philosopher can be confident that his system is true only if it receives social and political recognition. But in that case he cannot assume that the leaders and representatives of society and government will have received any special philosophical education.

A philosopher who takes his philosophy seriously must therefore try, in his own interest, to make it public. Writing an Introduction to Philosophy is justified not only for educational reasons, but for strictly philosophical reasons as well.
The author of a “phenomenological” or “dialectical” introduction to philosophy is, however, more modest than the authors of the introductions we are used to reading.

Those writers think that their Introduction exists mainly for the reader. If they themselves need it at all, this is only because they need an audience. The author of a Phenomenology, by contrast, believes that an “introduction to philosophy” is necessary first and foremost for himself.

This does not mean that he was previously a “non-philosopher” who had to learn the craft simply in order to understand philosophy “in general.” If that were all, he could simply use handbooks written by other authors, and there would be little reason for him to write a Phenomenology of his own.
No: his Phenomenology is indispensable because of his own philosophy, since only this Phenomenology can prepare him for that philosophy.

A Phenomenology is regarded as an absolutely necessary condition for understanding the philosophical system that follows it. But this means that the philosopher himself cannot understand that system without its corresponding Phenomenology. And if he cannot understand the system, still less can he write it.
Writing a Phenomenology is therefore an absolutely necessary condition for writing the system itself.

Phenomenology turns its own author into a philosopher—in a sense in which he was not one before. Before writing it, he was incapable of producing the new philosophical system that becomes possible only after the Phenomenology has been carried through.

So the author publishes his Phenomenology for his readers, both for educational reasons and so that its truth can be tested through social recognition. But he writes it—or thinks it through—for himself. Only after completing this preparatory phenomenological work can he move on to philosophy proper and actually become what he wants to be.

In this sense, a Phenomenology is the necessary first part of philosophy in the broad sense. It serves as the dialectical introduction to philosophy’s second, systematic part: philosophy in the narrower sense.

For contingent reasons, the first part may in practice remain without a sequel. But in principle the second part cannot appear without the first. A Phenomenology, as the dialectical introduction to a systematic philosophy, is just as inseparable from that philosophy as comparable introductions are inseparable from their corresponding “systems”—Plato’s dialectical Dialogues, for example; Descartes’s Meditations, with their method of doubt; or Kant’s Critiques.

And what is true of the author of a Phenomenology is equally true of its reader. Through it, the author prepares himself to write his philosophy; through the same work, the reader prepares himself to understand that philosophy. Since both are heading toward the same philosophy, both have to travel along the same path.
If the author of a Phenomenology is much more “humble” in this respect than the usual author of an Introduction to Philosophy, he is in another respect much more “arrogant.”

The usual introductions pursue very narrow and quite “modest” educational aims. But a philosopher who has passed through a Phenomenology necessarily addresses humanity as a whole and sees the appearance of his philosophy as a historical event of worldwide significance.
This “megalomania” comes from the very same source as his “modesty.”

The ordinary arrogance of philosophers—an arrogance that has often been mocked—comes from the fact that they think of themselves, more or less openly, as a kind of “superhuman” being. They imagine that they possess some special knowledge, acquired from who knows where, to which ordinary mortals have no access.

When they speak about themselves and their knowledge, they separate themselves from both the natural environment and the human world around them. Sometimes they claim to enjoy some immediate contact, outside space and time, with Reason, Intellect, or Spirit—something eternal, superhuman, and more or less divine. At other times they attribute their philosophical achievements to some special kind of “genius.”

They therefore imagine that they can somehow arrive at philosophy or “wisdom” without the help of any other human being and without any need for an Introduction. Such philosophers either never write an “Introduction” to their philosophy at all, or else write one only after they have already constructed that philosophy, out of condescending consideration for the weakness of ordinary mortals.

The phenomenologist, by contrast, is aware of his connection to the world. He knows that his philosophical knowledge depends on the natural and historical conditions of his existence, and that he has to learn philosophy like any other human being.
He therefore understands that the author must reach his philosophy by exactly the same phenomenological path as the reader, who is no less dependent on external conditions.

Once the phenomenologist regards himself as an “ordinary” human being, closely tied to his own time and therefore, through that time, to the whole history of humanity, he must also connect his philosophy with that history.
Born from history, philosophy returns to history.

The phenomenologist sees his philosophy as a product of its “time,” and therefore as one result of the collective effort of humanity as a whole—an effort which, for that very reason, concerns all humanity.

He writes a Phenomenology because he believes that existing philosophy has in some way been refuted by history, and because he assumes that no new philosophy can arise without the appearance of a Phenomenology corresponding to the new historical age.

The “non-philosophers” to whom the Phenomenology is addressed cannot therefore be some isolated group that happens, for reasons no one can quite explain, to be interested in philosophy. They are the whole historical age in question: humanity as it exists at that particular moment.

With the appearance of a philosophy prepared by a Phenomenology, it is not only its author, or some larger or smaller group of readers, that becomes philosophical. Humanity as a whole becomes philosophical.

And if we add that only a life that has become conscious of itself can properly be called human, and that this becoming-conscious is what we call philosophy, then we must say that a given historical age completes its development only when its philosophy appears.
The philosophy prepared by the Phenomenology gives that age a new life, because philosophy belongs to an age just as much as its economy, politics, science, art, and so on.

Phenomenology, then, is not merely intended for the non-philosopher who reads an Introduction to Philosophy in the usual sense, something designed to make philosophy “accessible to the public.” Nor is it merely intended for the philosopher as the “first, introductory or dialectical part of philosophy,” whose function is to make the second, systematic part possible.
It is also part of the world-historical process through which humanity genuinely develops.
In this sense, Phenomenology can be regarded as one stage on the “path to wisdom,” or, as Hegel puts it, as the “becoming of knowledge” (Werden des Wissens).

Like everything human, true human knowledge—and especially the knowledge human beings have of themselves, that is, philosophical knowledge—develops in time. It therefore has a history: the history of humanity understood precisely as the becoming of knowledge.
Every genuinely new stage in this development is therefore also a stage in history as a whole: a “historical age.”
And since a new philosophy cannot appear without its corresponding Phenomenology, the appearance of that Phenomenology must itself be regarded as a “historical event.”

In particular, the actual appearance of a socialist philosophy—and of the Phenomenology that leads to it—is just as decisive for our socialist age as the appearance of a socialist economy or a socialist state.
A philosopher who takes his philosophy seriously must therefore place his Phenomenology in a “historical” context.
This kind of philosophical “arrogance” is unavoidable. But it must never become personal arrogance.

The phenomenologist does not regard his philosophy as something he has personally “created.” He sees it as a product of his age. He knows that its “world-historical” importance is due not to his own “genius,” but exclusively to the place the philosophy occupies in world history and to the age to which it belongs.
That he personally happens to be its spokesman is a contingent fact, the result of his particular “abilities” or of other circumstances beyond his control.

His personal “modesty” appears in the fact that he does not judge the truth of his philosophy by his own opinion, or by the praise of a few disciples and “admirers,” but by whether or not it is recognized by the historical age itself—that is, by the real society that embodies that age.
In any case, a Phenomenology is a dialectical introduction to philosophy in three senses:

First, it turns its own author into a philosopher by making it possible for him, in principle, to answer philosophically every question that a person belonging to that historical age can ask about himself.
Second, it turns, in principle, any reader who understands it into a philosopher, by enabling that reader to understand these answers and make them his own.

Third, it transforms the historical age in which it appears. It turns a “non-philosophical” or “pre-philosophical” period into a “philosophical” one: an age that has become fully conscious of itself—or, more precisely, an age capable of becoming fully conscious of itself in a “systematic philosophy.”
The aim of Phenomenology is therefore to bring a new philosophy into being in its author, in its reader, and in the human being “in general.”

To understand this aim more fully, we need to know what kind of philosophy Phenomenology is trying to produce. But since we discussed this already in the first part of this “introduction,” it will be enough here simply to recall the main points.

First, philosophy must achieve the greatest possible self-awareness. It must in principle be capable of answering every question that can be asked today, and above all every question that can be asked about the human being, including the author of the philosophy himself.

Second, philosophical answers must be concrete. They must concern what actually exists, here and now, in the real material world—not what merely could or should exist, and not something that exists only in human consciousness.

Third, philosophical answers must belong not to the realm of more or less plausible opinion, but to knowledge in the fullest and strictest sense. They must not rest on “postulates” that we are asked to accept on faith, or on “axioms” that we are simply told to regard as “true” and that could just as easily be replaced by others. They must rest on statements that are absolutely true and that show themselves to be true.

In other words, philosophical discourse—conscious discourse about concrete reality—must not merely be articulate, meaningful, and coherent, or free from internal contradictions. In the strongest sense of the word, it must be convincing.

This threefold definition of philosophy, and of wisdom, lets us identify the three basic elements of the aim Phenomenology sets itself, each of which helps determine the character of Phenomenology itself.
Let us begin with the element of self-awareness.
We have seen that complete knowledge of any concrete reality is nothing other than perfect knowledge, or omniscience.
So when the philosopher tries to answer every concrete question about himself—that is, when he seeks the fullest possible self-awareness—he must in fact try to answer every possible question.
If so, then Phenomenology can turn the “non-philosopher” into a philosopher simply by making complete self-awareness possible.

In other words, Phenomenology must teach a human being—any human being—to ask every question that can be asked, under the historical conditions of the time, about himself, about his life in the real natural world, and about his real activity in the human world.

It must extend human self-consciousness to its furthest limits. It must bring the human being to a point where he is conscious of, and knows, everything that constitutes concrete or real human existence—an existence which, precisely because it is concrete, is conditioned by the full set of external conditions, both natural and historical.
Since self-consciousness is knowledge of oneself, that is, of one’s “I,” the first question Phenomenology must teach us to ask is this:
Where does the human “I” come from?
